+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                 DRAMA AS LITERARY FORM — LANDSCAPE               |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                  |
|  ORIGINS          CLASSICAL      RENAISSANCE    MODERN          |
|  -------          ---------      -----------    ------          |
|  Dionysian        Greek tragedy  Elizabethan    Naturalism       |
|  ritual           Greek comedy   Spanish Gold.  Expressionism    |
|  Dithyramb        Roman comedy   Italian opera  Brechtian epic   |
|  (choral hymn)    Latin mime     Commedia d.a.  Absurdism        |
|                                                                  |
|  THEORETICAL BACKBONE                                            |
|  --------------------                                            |
|  Aristotle's Poetics (c. 335 BCE) — the grammar of tragedy      |
|  Key concepts: mimesis, hamartia, anagnorisis, peripeteia,       |
|  catharsis, the unities, spectacle vs. story                     |
|                                                                  |
|  DRAMATIC SUBGENRES                                              |
|  Tragedy          comic relief? no — ends in death/disaster      |
|  Comedy           ends in marriage/reconciliation/celebration    |
|  Tragicomedy      elements of both; mixed ending                 |
|  Melodrama        heightened emotion, clear moral stakes         |
|  Farce            physical comedy, coincidence, improbability    |
|  Satire           ridicule with critical intent                  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

HAMARTIA — CORRECT UNDERSTANDING
----------------------------------
Not: moral flaw that deserves punishment
Yes: an error in action or judgment, often from ignorance

Why this matters:
  The tragic hero is not being punished for vice.
  Tragedy requires a good person falling through error.
  A wicked person getting just deserts is not tragedy —
  it is just punishment narrative.

Aristotle's requirement: the hero must be "intermediate"
  — not completely good (fall would be unjust and shocking)
  — not completely evil (fall would be satisfying, not pitiful)
  → Someone good, who makes an error, whose fall is undeserved

NATYASHASTRA (c. 200 BCE – 200 CE) — Bharata Muni
The foundational theory of Sanskrit theater: not just playwriting rules
but a complete performance theory covering movement, gesture, music, emotion.

RASA THEORY (the formal core):
  Theater's purpose: to produce rasa (aesthetic flavor/sentiment)
  in the audience — not emotion but aesthetic contemplation of emotion.

  8 (later 9) rasas:
    Shringara (love/beauty)    ← dominant in court drama
    Hasya (comedy/humor)
    Karuna (pathos/compassion)
    Raudra (fury)
    Vira (heroism)
    Bhayanaka (terror)
    Bibhatsa (disgust)
    Adbhuta (wonder)
    Shanta (peace/serenity)    ← 9th, added later

  Mapping: rasa ≈ a transfer function from performed
  emotion (bhava) to aesthetic experience in the audience.
  The actor does not feel the emotion; the actor encodes
  the permanent emotion (sthayi-bhava) via specific gestures
  (mudras) and expressions (abhinaya) to trigger rasa.

KALIDASA (c. 4th-5th century CE):
  Abhijnanasakuntalam (Shakuntala): the paradigmatic Sanskrit
  court drama. Recognition plot (abhijnana = recognition —
  compare Aristotle's anagnorisis). Protagonist: King
  Dushyanta must recognize Shakuntala as his wife.
  The dramatic engine is a curse that causes forgetting
  (suppressed recognition), lifted by a physical token
  (ring). Formal parallel to type-theoretic identity:
  the ring is a witness term for the identity proposition.
